cues.text: Section five looks at information technology as a source of competitive advantage.
Competitive advantage is the ability to deliver superior value, or to operate at lower cost than competitors, in a way that supports business success.
It is worth separating this from competitive parity, which means simply matching what the industry expects.
Consider a bank.
A mobile banking app may be necessary merely to remain competitive, because customers expect it.
But a superior fraud detection capability, together with personalised service, may be what actually differentiates the bank from its rivals.
Technology can support advantage in several ways.
It can support cost leadership, through automation and efficient infrastructure.
It can support differentiation, through unique customer experiences.
And it can support focus, through specialised services for a particular market.
Two related ideas are worth noting.
Scalability allows growth without a proportional increase in cost.
Customer stickiness arises when a service becomes valuable and convenient enough to retain its users, and importantly, that stickiness should not depend on unfair restrictions.
Next, the digital flywheel.
This is a reinforcing cycle.
Better service attracts users.
Usage produces useful data.
Analysis of that data improves the service.
And the improved service attracts more users, so the cycle continues.
For this to work, several things are required: consent, data quality, useful feedback, and actual improvements.
More data alone does not guarantee value.
Now we turn to Porter's Five Forces.
I will go through the table force by force, looking at how IT can change each one.
First, the threat of new entrants.
Scale, trusted platforms and integration can increase entry barriers.
Second, supplier bargaining power.
Procurement platforms and interoperable systems can broaden supplier choices.
Third, buyer bargaining power.
Personalised service and convenience can improve retention.
Fourth, the threat of substitutes.
Innovation can make an existing offering more useful than the alternatives.
Fifth, rivalry.
Analytics, automation and differentiated services can improve competitiveness.
However, technology can also strengthen competitors or lower barriers to entry.
Cloud infrastructure, for example, allows a startup to launch without building a data centre.
So the same technology can both enable and threaten established firms.
The next framework is the Resource-Based View, or RBV.
RBV explains advantage through internal resources and capabilities.
Within it, VRIO asks whether a resource is Valuable, Rare, difficult to Imitate, and supported by the Organisation.
Take commodity cloud servers: they are available to rivals, so they offer little distinctive advantage.
By contrast, a well-integrated proprietary dataset, a skilled team and trusted operating processes may be harder to reproduce.
And one qualification matters here: a valuable resource that is not organisationally exploited does not automatically yield advantage.
Finally, digital maturity.
Digital maturity describes how effectively an organisation integrates technology into its strategy, processes, culture and customer value.
A low-maturity organisation uses fragmented manual tools.
A more mature organisation integrates its systems, measures outcomes, and adapts continuously.
Remember that maturity is not a contest to buy the most advanced technology.
